title: Observation of baryon-number violation

concept.text: The innovation is a convincing experimental observation that a proton or a nucleon bound inside an atomic nucleus decays through a process that changes baryon number, the quantity that counts baryons minus antibaryons. A representative channel is p → e+ π0: a proton disappears and produces a positron and a neutral pion. Detecting such a decay would establish that nucleons can be unstable. The discovery sought here remains hypothetical; the supplied searches establish limits and background-compatible events.

Scope synthesis: the title covers baryon-number violation broadly, while this record's experimental target and completion criteria concern nucleon decay. Other baryon-number-violating processes could address the broader concept but would require their own signatures and discovery criteria. For nucleon decay, the essential achievement is a mode-specific signal statistically distinguishable from atmospheric-neutrino interactions and other backgrounds; the raw signal rate need not exceed the total background rate.

significance.text: A convincing observation would reveal a failure of baryon-number conservation and establish nucleon instability, providing a new experimental constraint on fundamental interactions. The supplied Super-Kamiokande paper describes grand-unified theories as generically predicting baryon-number-violating proton decay. A measured decay signature and partial lifetime would therefore provide powerful tests of such theories, although neither would uniquely identify a unified theory.

Interpretive synthesis: a partial lifetime would be a measured property of a particular decay channel, not a direct measurement of the unification energy scale. Translating it into an interaction scale would require a theoretical model and assumptions about its parameters. Similarly, observing one nucleon-decay channel would establish that form of instability without proving that all matter decays or determining every possible decay channel.

The Hyper-Kamiokande white paper motivates baryon-number violation as relevant to fundamental physics and cosmology. A laboratory discovery could inform explanations of the cosmic matter excess, but identifying which cosmological mechanism actually operated would require additional evidence. The supplied material establishes no immediate technological application; the direct advance would be knowledge of fundamental interactions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is detecting and identifying extremely rare nucleon decay with enough evidence to separate it from ordinary interactions that mimic its final state. The scale of the challenge is illustrated by Super-Kamiokande's lower bound of τ/B(p → e+ π0) > 2.4 × 10^34 years at 90% confidence. Here τ/B is the partial lifetime, conventionally expressed as the total lifetime divided by the branching fraction for that channel. This bound is neither an observed lifetime nor a limit applying equally to every nucleon-decay mode.

The concrete experimental barriers include accumulating sufficient target mass and observation time, reconstructing the relevant particles, and controlling atmospheric-neutrino backgrounds and detector uncertainties. For the fully visible p → e+ π0 channel, reconstructed invariant mass and total momentum provide important discrimination. Super-Kamiokande's documented selections included 800 < Mtot < 1050 MeV/c² and Ptot < 250 MeV/c. These are analysis selections for that search, not universal discovery requirements.

Engineering synthesis: discovery also requires credible signal efficiencies, detector-response calibration, and uncertainty estimates for interactions inside nuclei. Different final states pose different reconstruction problems. In p → ν̄ K+, the neutrino is unobserved, so identification must rely on the observable kaon and its decay products, interpreted with the missing neutrino accounted for. Increasing exposure alone cannot resolve an inadequately understood background. The supplied evidence does not establish a guaranteed lifetime range in which a signal must appear.

current_state.text: Takenaka et al.'s 2020 Super-Kamiokande analysis used 450 kiloton-years of data collected from April 1996 through May 2018. It found no p → e+ π0 candidates and set τ/B(p → e+ π0) > 2.4 × 10^34 years at 90% confidence. This is a demonstrated exclusion in a specified channel and dataset, not evidence that baryon number is conserved under all circumstances. The supplied review assessed the complete paper text for this result.

The supplied April 2026 three-body pion search reported one candidate event in each of p → e+ π0 π0 and p → μ+ π0 π0, consistent with the expected atmospheric-neutrino background. Its arXiv submission history records an initial submission on 13 April 2026 and a revision on 16 April. The supplied review assessed the landing-page abstract and submission history rather than the full paper. Although the source index also lists a saved PDF, its presence does not extend what that review established. The asserted journal-publication date of 26 October 2026 remains unverified; the April preprint dates do not disprove a later journal publication.

The 2022 Hyper-Kamiokande Snowmass white paper projects proton-decay sensitivity of order 10^35 years for p → e+ π0 with 20 years of data. This is a design projection, not achieved sensitivity or an observation. The supplied review found the numerical projection in the extracted text accompanying the figure caption, so this statement does not depend on an independent reading of the figure curves.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material does not establish the earlier assertion about a 2024 p → e+/μ+ η search, specify which simplest unified models are excluded, or quantify how far surviving models extend beyond planned detectors' reach. Those assertions remain unverified rather than disproved. The documented results above also do not establish comprehensive coverage of all developments through 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: obtain a statistically compelling sample of mode-specific nucleon-decay candidates, using 5σ as a proposed discovery threshold for this record. The analysis should account for background and detector uncertainties and show that the excess remains credible under reasonable alternative background treatments. Neither 5σ nor a particular event count is established here as a mandatory field-wide standard. A stronger lower limit on partial lifetime would improve the search but would not demonstrate decay.
completion_criteria.label: Mode-specific nucleon-decay excess reaches 5σ under alternative background treatments

completion_criteria.text: For p → e+ π0, a convincing demonstration should reconstruct an invariant mass and total momentum compatible with the expected nucleon-decay signature, with detector resolution and nuclear effects accounted for. Super-Kamiokande's existing use of mass and momentum selections provides a concrete basis for this proposed test, without making its numerical cuts requirements for every future detector or analysis.
completion_criteria.label: Positron–pion invariant mass and total momentum match nucleon decay

completion_criteria.text: Proposed channel-specific and reproducibility requirements: for p → ν̄ K+, establish a consistent signature using the observable kaon and its decay products, without treating the final state as fully visible. Document the exposure, event selections, efficiencies, calibration, background estimates, and uncertainty treatment sufficiently for independent scrutiny and analysis reproduction. Check that the result is robust across relevant detector conditions and reasonable analysis variations.
completion_criteria.label: Antineutrino–kaon decay signature is robust, documented and independently reproducible

completion_criteria.text: Independent confirmation in a complementary detector technology, such as liquid argon, would strengthen confidence by testing the signal with different detection capabilities and systematic uncertainties. The Hyper-Kamiokande white paper explicitly discusses complementarity with liquid-argon detectors. Such confirmation would still need its own convincing evidence; a second technology does not automatically make a result secure.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Complementary detector technology independently confirms the nucleon-decay signal

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: completion would establish the observed channel or channels over the demonstrated experimental conditions. Finite datasets would not establish every possible baryon-violating process or a unique underlying theory. Inferring a unification scale and explaining the cosmic baryon density would remain separate interpretive and experimental tasks.
completion_criteria.label: Conclusions remain limited to observed channels and demonstrated conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis — PHY-13, A tested mechanism for the cosmic matter excess: nucleon decay would provide laboratory evidence relevant to baryon-violating explanations of the matter–antimatter imbalance. PHY-07 asks whether a specified baryon-violating process occurs; PHY-13 asks which mechanism generated the observed cosmic excess and whether that account is quantitatively and cosmologically supported. Completing PHY-07 would not complete PHY-13 or automatically constrain every proposed mechanism.

Roster synthesis — PHY-08, Observation of lepton-number violation: the distinction is useful but not absolute. The example channels p → e+ π0 and p → ν̄ K+ change lepton number as well as baryon number, so one observation could bear on both concepts. Conversely, evidence of lepton-number violation need not establish nucleon decay or baryon-number violation. The entries retain distinct experimental targets.

Roster synthesis — PHY-06, Discovery of a magnetic monopole: monopole searches and proton-decay searches can both test ideas associated with unification, but they seek different phenomena. A monopole discovery would establish a new magnetic object; nucleon decay would establish a baryon-number-violating transition. Neither observation would by itself demonstrate the other.

change_log.change: Preserved PHY-07 and its title while clarifying that the proposed demonstration targets nucleon decay within the broader category of baryon-number violation.
change_log.reason: Maintains concept identity and makes the narrower experimental scope explicit.

change_log.change: Replaced a requirement for a rate above background with statistical distinguishability from background.
change_log.reason: Discovery depends on the significance and interpretation of the signal, not simply on exceeding the total background rate.

change_log.change: Retained the 2.4 × 10^34-year bound with its channel, confidence level, exposure, data interval, and partial-lifetime interpretation.
change_log.reason: These quantitative details are supported and distinguish an exclusion limit from an observed lifetime.

change_log.change: Qualified the claims about excluded simplest unified models, surviving-model reach, and universally accessible Standard Model processes.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish those broad assertions; their limitations do not invalidate the discovery target.

change_log.change: Replaced direct measurement of a unification scale with model-dependent inference from a decay signature and partial lifetime.
change_log.reason: A lifetime alone does not determine the underlying interaction scale or uniquely identify a theory.

change_log.change: Narrowed the impact from universal matter instability to demonstrated nucleon instability and clarified the conditional relevance to baryogenesis.
change_log.reason: An observed channel would not establish all forms of matter instability or identify the cosmological mechanism.

change_log.change: Separated fully visible e+ π0 reconstruction from ν̄ K+ identification and added concrete experimental barriers.
change_log.reason: An unobserved neutrino prevents treating both channels as equivalent invariant-mass reconstructions.

change_log.change: Presented 5σ, reproducibility requirements, and complementary confirmation as proposed completion criteria.
change_log.reason: The sources motivate these tests but do not establish them as necessary or sufficient consensus standards.

change_log.change: Retained the April 2026 three-body candidates and preprint chronology while leaving the October journal date unverified.
change_log.reason: The assessed abstract supports background-compatible candidates; its submission history does not establish or disprove later journal publication.

change_log.change: Preserved the Hyper-Kamiokande 20-year, order-10^35-year projection and explained the review's access boundaries.
change_log.reason: Projected sensitivity must remain distinct from achieved performance, and a saved but unassessed PDF cannot supply additional findings.

change_log.change: Integrated distinctions among PHY-06, PHY-08, and PHY-13 without merging entries.
change_log.reason: Shared theoretical motivation and overlapping quantum-number changes do not make their experimental goals identical.

unresolved_issues: Which specific unified models are excluded by the cited limits, and which surviving parameter ranges lie beyond planned detector sensitivities? No model-specific comparison is supplied.
The stated 2024 p → e+/μ+ η result lacks a supporting supplied source.
The claimed 26 October 2026 journal-publication date for the three-body pion search remains unverified, rather than disproved.

The source index lists a full PDF for the April 2026 search, but the supplied review assessed only its landing-page abstract and submission history; no additional full-paper conclusions can be incorporated.

brief.title: Evidence that protons can decay
possible: Scientists could establish that particles inside atomic nuclei can decay. They would identify a proton, or another nuclear particle, disappearing into other particles and measure how often that particular decay happens.
why: For physicists, this would reveal a failure of a conservation rule: the number of nuclear particles minus their antimatter counterparts stays constant. It would give them a new way to test theories that bring fundamental forces together.

sources.showed: They found no candidates for a proton decaying into a positron and a neutral pion. These are the particles sought as the decay products. The search set a lower bound on how rarely this decay could happen.
sources.quote: No candidates have been found for p→ e+π0
sources.cited_for: This search demonstrates a limit on a particular proton decay, with no observed signal.
sources.not_established: A lower lifetime bound does not establish that protons decay or that every possible decay is absent.

sources.showed: A preprint reported candidates in searches for a proton decaying into a charged antimatter particle and neutral pions. The candidates were consistent with ordinary interactions.
sources.quote:
These limits are more than one order of magnitude better than those of the
previous experiment.
sources.cited_for: Searches for other proton decays have also produced limits rather than a convincing signal.
sources.not_established: The candidates do not distinguish proton decay from interactions caused by neutrinos from the atmosphere.

sources.who: J. Bian and colleagues, on behalf of the Hyper-Kamiokande Collaboration
sources.showed: They projected how much further Hyper-Kamiokande could search for proton decay and described how detectors using liquid argon would complement it.
sources.cited_for: Larger searches and different detector technologies offer complementary ways to pursue proton decay.
sources.not_established: Projected sensitivity is neither achieved performance nor evidence that a decay will occur within reach.

shown: Super-Kamiokande has placed strong limits on particular proton decays. Its search for a positron and a neutral pion found no candidates. Other searches found candidates consistent with neutrinos, particles whose interactions can mimic decay. No convincing nuclear-particle decay has been observed.
missing: A convincing decay signal must stand apart from ordinary interactions that imitate it.
Detectors must collect enough observations while reliably identifying the particles left by a decay.
Researchers must establish detection efficiency and account for detector errors and interactions inside nuclei.

milestones.label: A decay signal survives alternative background estimates
milestones.explanation: A particular decay would have to reach the proposed 5-sigma statistical threshold while remaining convincing under alternative estimates of mimicking events. This would separate discovery from a stronger limit.

milestones.label: The positron and pion match a decaying nuclear particle
milestones.explanation: The positron and neutral pion would have to yield the expected combined mass and total momentum, their combined motion, accounting for detector and nuclear effects. This would test whether they came from the proposed decay.

milestones.label: The kaon signal withstands scrutiny and reproduction
milestones.explanation: A decay involving a kaon, an observable particle, and an unseen antineutrino would need a robust signature and enough detail for independent analysis reproduction. This would make its interpretation testable.

milestones.label: A different detector technology independently confirms the signal
milestones.explanation: A detector using a complementary technology would have to find convincing evidence of the decay independently. This would test the signal with different detection capabilities and sources of error.

milestones.label: Conclusions stay within what the observed decays establish
milestones.explanation: Conclusions would have to remain limited to the observed decays and demonstrated conditions. This would keep a discovery from being mistaken for proof of a unique theory or the fate of all matter.

uncertain: The discovery threshold and confirmation requirements need to suit the particular decay, detector and uncertainties.
No guaranteed decay rate places a signal within planned detectors’ reach.
A discovery could inform explanations of the universe’s matter excess, but identifying its cause would require additional evidence.
